courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
md: The OWASP API Security Top 10 warns that comparing the session's user id with an id parameter covers only a small subset of BOLA cases. Objects are often shared (a team folder, a manager viewing a report), so the real question is "may this user perform this action on this object under our policy", which lessons 11 and 12 turn into one reusable check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
md: Central does not mean single. Next.js apps that checked access only in middleware were exposed when CVE-2025-29927 let requests skip middleware (lesson 7). Decide policy in one place, but enforce it at more than one layer: at the route, and again at the data (scoped queries, RLS).

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Moving a service account to AES is not a fix by itself. An AES ticket for `Summer2019!` is still crackable; it only costs more per guess. The fix is a password nobody can guess: a gMSA or a long random secret.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
md: In AD a certificate trusted for client authentication is a password that survives password resets. ESC1 is a template that lets any user choose the name in the certificate. Audit templates, treat CAs as Tier 0, watch 4886 and 4887 for mismatched subjects, and revoke rather than reset.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: OOXML: a zip of XML parts, and links that fetch remote content
md: A document can be dangerous with zero bytes of code inside it. In OOXML, read every .rels part: one line with TargetMode External can be the whole attack.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: An empty sandbox report means 'not observed in this environment', never 'benign'. Say exactly that in your notes and in any verdict you hand to the SOC.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: OPSEC through the defender's eyes: every action leaves a trace
md: Map each emulated step to the log that must record it before the exercise. If the step passes unseen, the gap is in one of three places: the data was never collected, it was collected but no rule looked, or a rule fired and nobody acted. Lesson 12 names these gaps.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Workflow: capture once with an interposer, analyze with a heap profiler to find what to fix in code, convert to a workload, then replay that one workload against each allocator or tuning and compare RSS against ideal RSS.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: OAuth is about **authorization**: letting a client act on a user's behalf with limited scope. The access token is meant for the resource server, not for the client to learn who the user is. Logging users in needs OpenID Connect (lesson 10).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Misconception: "we validate the token at the API gateway, so services can just decode it." Then any path around the gateway, and any token for another audience the gateway also accepts, reaches services that trust it blindly. Each service should at least check the audience meant for it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: "Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
md: No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Metrics that matter: time to remediate, open age and coverage
md: Measure what is still open and what you cannot see. Mean time to remediate, open age, SLA compliance and coverage together describe a programme; any one alone can be gamed by accident.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: `volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and cost parameters
md: Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, or bcrypt for legacy), a unique salt per user, and a cost tuned as high as your login traffic allows. Record the parameters with each hash, and raise them over time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Passkeys and WebAuthn: why phishing stops working
md: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser binds every signature to the real site's origin and the credential to the site's domain. The user's judgment is not part of the security argument.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Rust binaries: mangled paths, slices and panics
md: In Rust binaries, follow the panics. Every `panic_bounds_check`, `unwrap` failure and `expect` message carries a source location or message string. Even when symbols are stripped, cross-references to those strings map functions back to files and lines in the original crate.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
md: Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, the godbolt.org website that shows the assembly a compiler produces, or the `-S` flag, which makes the compiler write assembly instead of an object file) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: Resilience is the outcome; continuity is about business processes; contingency and disaster recovery are about systems and sites. A real organisation needs a small family of plans that agree with each other on who decides, in what order things come back, and who speaks.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: Every backup needs an owner, a check on every step, an alert on missing success through a separate channel, and an automated restore test that measures time and verifies content. Rehearsed restores (Gmail 2011) produce estimates; unrehearsed ones (GitLab 2017) produce surprises.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: Draw the dependency graph of recovery itself and look for cycles. Break them with out-of-band copies (exported keys, printed runbooks, separate comms), break-glass accounts that depend on nothing in the estate, and tested access paths for every security tool you will need on the worst day.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
md: A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Learning where to cut: from character models to H-Net
md: The design space for byte models is who decides the cut: a fixed rate, a hand-written rule, a separate model (BLT), or the model's own loss (H-Net's cosine router plus a ratio loss). Learned cuts remove BLT's separately trained entropy model, at the cost of new machinery to make a discrete choice trainable.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
md: Matching the real model's outputs exactly on prompt $p$ does not mean the local replacement model uses the same mechanism. The paper compares it to a Taylor approximation: it agrees at the point and drifts as you move away, which is why interventions are needed later.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript
md: The URL fragment (everything after `#`) is never sent to the server, as MDN's URL guide notes. A DOM XSS that reads `location.hash` leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF. It has to be found in the JavaScript itself, by code review, by tests, or by browser-side tools such as DOM Invader, a tool preinstalled as an extension in Burp Suite's built-in browser that tracks sources reaching sinks.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Azure and Google Cloud: activity, resource and audit logs
md: Misconception: "the activity log shows who read the secret". It shows who changed the vault's access policy. Reading a secret is a data plane operation that appears only in Key Vault resource logs, and only if a diagnostic setting was sending them before the read.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containing without breaking production, and a cloud IR runbook
md: Contain in one coordinated window: close the source, revoke sessions and keys, cut the destination if needed, with production owners ready for the blip. Revocation without closing the source lets the attacker fetch fresh credentials; closing the source without revocation leaves stolen ones working.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Human access: LastPass 2022, Identity Center and break-glass
md: "We have MFA, so stolen passwords do not matter" is the misconception LastPass disproves. MFA protects the sign-in it guards. Long-lived access keys, keys stored in notes and anything readable from an already compromised device are outside its reach. Remove standing credentials, require phishing-resistant MFA, and treat engineer endpoints as part of production.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Least privilege, wildcards and the Capital One role
md: `"Resource": "*"` is not always a mistake (a few actions, such as `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, have no narrower resource), but `"Action": "*"` or `"service:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` in an application's role almost always is. Treat each one as a finding that needs a written reason.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: End to end: grouping a million log lines into named failure patterns
md: Cluster names come from word statistics, not from causes. Two messages from different systems that share a phrase will land together, and one rare but critical message can hide inside a big cluster. Always read a few members of every cluster, and treat the HDBSCAN noise set as a queue to review, not a bin to discard.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: Vectorized engines split work into type-specialized primitives over arrays, and pass filters along as lists of positions instead of moving data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: Misconception: "it works at -O0, so -O2 has a compiler bug." Compiler bugs exist, but UB in the program is far more common. And -O0 is no safe harbor: GCC folds `a + b < a` to `b < 0` even at -O0, and the next compiler version may exploit UB that this one ignores.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Measure time with repetitions, medians and spreads, on representative input, one change at a time. Explain each gain with counters and compiler remarks. On this program LTO gave the big win, PGO a few percent, and -O3 and -mcpu=native nothing measurable.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain squared-error regression (the L2 loss) to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: A central lookup table (key range to server) also gives minimal movement, and many databases use one. The catch is that every client must fetch and agree on the table. Consistent hashing lets each client compute the owner from the key and the server list alone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: Misconception: "root in a container is harmless because it is only container root". Without user namespaces, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp and the LSM. Remove those fences, or find a bug in them, and it is real root.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Hardened default for application pods: no token, non-root, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, explicit writable volumes, resource limits, image by digest.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Misconception: "the database is internal, so it is not exposed". Internal means reachable by every pod in the cluster unless a policy says otherwise. Treat the pod network as a hostile network.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: Legal line: everything in this course is for clusters you own or have written permission to test. Scanning the internet for open kubelets or Docker APIs, or using one you find, is unauthorised access under laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act, whatever the intent.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
md: Each test rules out one failure class, nothing more. A CoT that passes truncation and mistake tests is causally used, but it can still omit a factor (as in Turpin's hints). Lanham et al. call this a defense-in-depth approach: no single test certifies faithfulness.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
md: Set the threshold from a false-positive budget on clean runs, report recall at that FPR, and expect low precision when misbehavior is rare. Score CoT and actions separately and combine them: the CoT catches subtle intent, the actions keep a persuasive CoT from talking the monitor out of an obvious flag.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
md: An IV or nonce is an input with a contract (unique, sometimes unpredictable), not a constant. When a design fixes it, ask what the mode's security proof assumes, who controls the plaintext, and how many attempts an attacker gets. Better: use a standard authenticated protocol instead of designing one.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: Under section 1 a failed attempt can be enough: the offence is about intent and knowledge, not success. 'I didn't get in' is not a defence to trying.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: "It's only code" is not an export defence. Sending exploit technology abroad can need a licence, and US rules also cover releasing controlled technology to foreign persons at home (a "deemed export", which the 2021 rule names). Disclosure to the people who will fix the bug is the carved-out case; selling capability is not.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: "Nobody asked me directly" is weak protection. Misprision is about *active concealment* of a known felony, and obstruction can be committed by causing others not to disclose. Changing records, drafting the NDA and signing statements you know mislead are acts, not silence.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: Epochs = weight x budget / unique tokens. Up to about 4 epochs repetition costs almost nothing; beyond that each pass is worth less, and by about 40 it is worthless. Cap epochs per domain and give the surplus to domains that still have unique data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
md: Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
md: GitHub's environment docs note that workflows on self-hosted runners are not run in an isolated container, even if they use environments. An environment controls when a secret is released, not what else on that machine can read it afterwards. Pair environments with clean runners (lesson 3).

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
md: Deleting a file usually removes the *pointer* to the data, not the data. Recovery works until the space is reused. Everything in the first half of this course is a variation on that sentence.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
md: Encryption turns *keep it running* into the first forensic step. If you arrive at a decrypted, unlocked machine, you may never get that state back.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly (the trainable $\pi_\theta$, with weights $\theta$) and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
md: DPO is a strong, cheap offline baseline, not a strict upgrade over RL. Its blind spot is everything the policy generates that the pairs never covered. Fresh on-policy pairs, whether per round (iterative) or per step (online), close much of the gap; tuned on-policy RL still wins in some settings.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
md: MFA protects the login, not the session. Anything that leaks or steals a session token after login bypasses MFA completely, which is why session lifetime, session binding and killing sessions after an incident matter.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
md: A device that can no longer be patched, or that you cannot trust after a compromise, is not a vulnerability to manage: it is a replacement to schedule. Track support dates like expiry dates and replace before them.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
md: Misconception: "kernel mode makes a sensor untouchable." A kernel sensor can see everything, but so can any other code that reaches the kernel. An attacker who loads their own driver, or abuses a vulnerable signed one, is on equal footing with the sensor. That is exactly what the EDR-killer lesson covers.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
md: These controls each close one path: LAPS stops one local password from opening every machine; LSA protection stops ordinary processes reading LSASS; Credential Guard keeps the most reusable secrets out of LSASS's reach entirely; the ASR LSASS rule covers machines that can run neither. Check they are actually running, not just configured.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Misconception: an attacker needs an admin to consent before an app can steal mail. Delegated mail and file permissions are user-consentable by default, and the user's own mailbox is often the prize. Admin consent is needed for the tenant-wide versions, which is why attackers who compromise an admin go straight for application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: Misconception: a device-based Conditional Access rule means only company laptops get in. It means the token request came with a valid device identity. A device an attacker registers is a real device object, which is why device registration and join rights should be restricted and new registrations reviewed.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Misconception: after a help-desk takeover, resetting the victim's password and MFA again evicts the attacker. If the attacker federated a domain or added an app credential, they can mint access without that account. Check federation settings, app credentials, role assignments and registered devices before calling it contained.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
md: ASLR is a secret, and like any secret it fails when leaked or when there are too few bits to stop guessing. Count the bits, avoid restart patterns that keep the secret constant, and treat information leaks as the first half of an exploit.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
md: Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats
md: More levels are not free. The cascade API docs warn that adding levels is not always beneficial because of the overhead of merging attention results, and the paper notes real shared prefixes are often shorter than the long-prefix kernel benchmarks.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLC: breadth-first search over every reachable state
md: Liveness is only checked if you ask. In the CACM paper's table of results, a lock-free data structure spec "improved confidence" but missed a liveness bug because liveness was not checked. Also remember the bounded model: no error at N = 3 says nothing about N = 4.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
md: Verification moves trust from "we tested enough" to "the spec says the right thing". Spend your review effort on the spec: the invariants, the environment actions you modeled, and every assumption or trusted function.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
md: A 2x faster GEMM is not a 2x faster step: the speedup is capped by the non-GEMM share of time and eaten into by casting overhead. FP8 GEMM inputs also save almost no memory; the bytes live in master weights, gradients and optimizer state, and in communication, which need their own FP8 treatment (shared scales, automatic scaling).

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: "The data was public anyway" was not a defence. Each field may be visible on a profile, but linking a phone number to a name at scale creates a new data set the users never published. Regulators judge the feature design, not just whether a password was stolen.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: Each verification step also costs honest people: those without a phone of their own, without a bank card, or without the right documents. Put the expensive steps in front of the high-value actions they protect, and offer an alternative path.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Do not train on chargebacks as if they arrived on the day of the payment. Recent payments look clean simply because their disputes have not arrived yet; a model trained on last week's data learns that last week had no fraud.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Enforcement, explanations and appeals
md: Enforce on a proportionate ladder, give a statement of the policy and behaviour (not the detector's thresholds), let a different person review appeals, and treat overturns as labels.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
md: After fsync fails on buffered data, assume the dirty data is gone. Do not retry and continue: recover from a log you know is durable. That is why PostgreSQL's [data_sync_retry](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-error-handling.html) defaults to off, which turns such a failure into a PANIC and a WAL replay.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: To compare two fuzzing setups: 30 or more runs each, at least 24 hours, the same documented seeds, a statistical test, and bugs counted by distinct fixes. Anything less is an anecdote.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Publishing a working exploit is a separate, debated decision (OWASP notes both sides). It is never needed to get a memory-safety bug fixed: the sanitizer report and minimised input are proof. This course's path ends at the fix and the advisory.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
md: Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Misconception: latitude and longitude are x and y on a flat grid. They are angles on a sphere. Any shortcut that treats them as planar (Euclidean distance on degrees, fixed-size degree boxes) is wrong by a factor of $1/\cos\varphi$ in the east-west direction and breaks at 180 degrees longitude and near the poles.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Reusing a freed block on the same stream is safe without synchronization because stream order already serializes the old and new users. Cross-stream reuse needs events: record_stream in PyTorch, event dependencies in cudaMallocAsync pools.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: **Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
md: Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: The headline result is GraphRAG versus vector RAG on global sensemaking questions: 72 to 83% comprehensiveness win rates on Podcast. Against map-reduce over raw text, the advantage is small; the bigger win there is token cost at query time.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns
md: Hindsight makes every incident look obvious. At the time, the engineers involved were usually competent people working with the knowledge and trade-offs of their day. Read each case asking "what would have had to be true for this to be caught?", not "how could they be so careless?"

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book
md: Mass mailers exploited trust in three things at once: the sender (a friend's address), the file (a hidden extension) and the program (Outlook let scripts read addresses and send mail). Each fix removed one trust: show real extensions, block executable attachments, and make programs ask before using your address book or sending.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update
md: "It looked like ransomware, so paying would have restored our data" was wrong here. Kaspersky showed the attackers could not decrypt the disks. Classify destructive incidents by what the code does, not by what the ransom screen says.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
md: A percentage in parentheses after a `perf stat` line, like `(74.98%)`, means that event ran only that fraction of the time and was scaled. Treat such numbers as estimates, and be most suspicious when the workload has phases.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
md: An enclave or TEE protects against software that cannot reach its memory. It does not remove side channels: if enclave code runs on the same core as the attacker, its cache footprint, branch history and timing are as observable as any other program's. Enclave code must still be constant-time.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: HTTP/2 framing, and how downgrading brings desync back
md: HTTP/2 removes framing ambiguity only while the request stays HTTP/2. Every downgrade to HTTP/1.1 must enforce RFC 9113's rules before writing text: content-length equals the DATA total, no connection-specific fields, no CR, LF or NUL in names or values.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
md: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on different documents. BM25 misses paraphrases; dense retrieval blurs exact identifiers, codes and rare names. Fusing the lists recovers documents either one would miss and promotes documents both agree on.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Federation replaces many passwords with one trust decision per app: accept whatever this IdP's key signs, after checking it was meant for me, now. Every attack in this course breaks one of those three parts: the key, the checks, or the moment.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
md: Treat the IdP's signing keys and the configuration that says which IdPs and keys are trusted as tier 0 (Microsoft's name for the assets that control every identity in an organisation): the same protection as domain controllers (the servers that hold Active Directory's accounts and keys). Anyone who can change either can become any user without touching a password.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule
md: Session security cannot exceed device security. PAM, bastions and JIT protect the path; the PAW protects its start. Decide at a policy engine using identity, device and approval together, issue short-lived credentials, and enforce at one point.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
md: Isolating a host is not the same as stopping damage on it. NIST's example: a process that pings a remote host and, when the ping fails after disconnection, encrypts the disk. Capture what you need first when you can.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels
md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS (few I/O operations per second), bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device secrets: per-device keys, secure elements and House of Keys
md: Design rule: the worst outcome of fully compromising one unit should be the loss of that unit. Achieve it with per-device keys generated on the device, public keys in the cloud, and no shared secrets in firmware.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
md: `--disable-proto` is a useful second layer, not the fix: our test shows the `constructor.prototype` route still pollutes with it on. Fix the write (own keys, refused names, null-prototype objects); add the flag as defence in depth.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: The server-client boundary: Server Actions, secrets and bundles
md: Do not treat arguments of a Server Action as typed or trusted because TypeScript declared their types. TypeScript types disappear at run time; the POST body can contain anything. Validate arguments with a schema inside the action, exactly as you would for a REST endpoint.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
md: Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone, its single most likely class (pseudo-labeling), is not the same thing in general (lesson 9 shows one setting where top-1 targets did well). It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: On-policy distillation in code: student samples, teacher scores
md: For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch, and per-token reverse KL turns the teacher into a dense, per-token reward.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Offloading does not make attention read from CPU memory. In reuse offloading, blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the attention kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What offloading buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: Happened-before means *information could have flowed* from a to b through process order and messages. It is a partial order: many pairs of events are simply concurrent, and no clock reading can change that.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token
md: Why max and not average? The ColBERT ablation (an experiment that swaps out one component, retrains, and measures what changes) replaced max with average similarity and MRR@10 dropped noticeably. In the toy, the *founded* row of Doc A averages (0.03 + 0.02 + 0.18 + 0.98 + 0.49) / 5 = 0.34, even though the document contains a near-perfect match. Averaging punishes documents for having other content.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: n continuous thoughts cost n sequential forward passes at inference and n + 1 sequential passes per training example, with no tokens emitted for the latent steps.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Choose by what the extra slots carry. Fixed pause or filler embeddings add width within one pass. Coconut's fed-back hidden states and written CoT add serial depth across passes. Recurrent depth adds serial depth inside the network without any extra tokens.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
md: Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
md: RankNet does not need graded labels, only a set of preferred pairs. Burges notes the pairs can even be inconsistent, for example from a confused judge who prefers U1 to U2, U2 to U3 and U3 to U1.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
md: Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: `chmod 777` is not a fix for "permission denied". It lets every account on the machine, including a compromised web server account, modify the file. If a script run by root is world-writable, any user can make root run their code. Find the account that actually needs access and grant only that.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
md: A signal handler can interrupt any line of code, so it must only do async-signal-safe work, and a fix must be guarded by a test or it can quietly disappear in a refactor, as this one did after 14 years.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Automating a benchmark: SCAP, OpenSCAP and ComplianceAsCode
md: Running every generated fix at once on production is the fastest way to lock yourself out: the same playbook also changes PAM lockout rules, SSH ciphers and firewall policy. Generate, read, tailor, and roll out in stages (next lesson).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: When audit falls behind: backlog, lost events and full disks
md: Size the backlog for bursts (8192 is the packaged default on Ubuntu), choose the failure and disk actions deliberately (availability versus completeness), ship records off the host continuously, and alert on lost > 0 and on hosts that go silent.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
md: "It is only a miner" is the wrong conclusion. The same access that runs XMRig stole cloud credentials and SSH keys in both cases, and TeamTNT reused them to reach new systems. Treat cryptojacking as a full root compromise.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
md: LLM-as-judge for relevance is a measurement instrument. Like any instrument, you calibrate it against a trusted reference (human gold labels) before you read numbers off it.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
md: Do not rank by raw win percentage when models faced different opponents: beating weak models inflates it. BT accounts for who played whom. And never report a ranking without intervals; with few votes, neighbouring models are often statistically tied.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a prompt: rules, delimited inputs and the task
md: A good prompt separates three things the model must not confuse: the rules (stable), the input data (fenced in tags), and the task (stated plainly, ideally last). Then measure: every vendor guide says prompting is iterative and should be checked against test cases.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
md: The `minimum_should_match` default depends on context. In Elasticsearch it is 1 only when the bool has `should` clauses and no `must` or `filter` clauses; otherwise it is 0, and the should clauses become optional score boosts. Put Berlin and remote as bare should clauses next to a filter list and *every* city passes.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: Output tokens are the expensive kind for latency. Prefer designs whose answer is one token or one logit: pointwise labels, PRP in scoring mode, or FIRST-style first-token ranking.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
md: Pick the formulation by its failure mode: pointwise needs calibration, pairwise needs many calls, listwise needs a long context and a good initial order. Most practical gains come from controlling those failure modes (swapping, shuffling, cascades, distillation), not from a cleverer single prompt.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: Judge a match by how much better it is than the runner-up, not by its absolute distance. The ratio d1/d2 adapts to how distinctive each descriptor is.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: CAS compares bits, not history. Any lock-free algorithm that frees or reuses nodes must either version its pointers or guarantee that no thread can still hold a reference to a node that gets reused.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: Parsing accuracy is not the goal; downstream behaviour is. SHISO parsed 93 percent of messages into the right groups and still produced 7 times the false alarms, because the templates it got wrong were ones the detector was sensitive to. Always evaluate a parser change by re-running the task that consumes its output.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Time: clocks, time zones and the order of events
md: Daylight saving time makes 'local time' worse: once a year, an hour of local timestamps happens twice. Two events at 01:30 local on that night cannot be ordered without the offset. Log in UTC.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, the TPU inter-chip interconnect or ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
md: A looped model can quietly stop using its loop. If it learns to ignore $\mathbf{s}$, extra iterations do nothing. Track validation loss at several iteration counts (Huginn tracked 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64) during training, not just at the default.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: A d90 of 200 does not mean that 200 hand-picked weights would do. The 200 numbers are projected through a dense random map, so every original weight still moves a little. And 90% of full performance is the bar, not 100%.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally
md: Certified removal asks that the edited model be distributed almost like a model retrained without the point, within a factor $e^{\varepsilon}$. For L2-regularized linear models a Newton step plus training-time noise achieves it cheaply. For LLMs no such certificate exists.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Toward robust unlearning: tamper resistance, distillation, filtering
md: Output-level unlearning leaves the capability in the weights. The robust routes either train against attacks (TAR), move the behaviour into weights that never held the capability (distillation, UNDO), or never train on the content (filtering); each costs more compute or more planning.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Breaking TCC: $HOME poisoning, powerdir and XCSSET
md: All three bugs answer the same question wrongly: *who is asking, and where are their rules?* Fixes moved from trusting caller-controlled inputs ($HOME, the directory record, the bundle path) to checking the code that is actually running.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: A Mac hardening baseline, and where to practise
md: A Mac is well defended when every control from this course is on, managed, and observed: on by default (SIP, SSV, XProtect), switched on and escrowed (FileVault), constrained by policy (Gatekeeper, PPPC, login items), and watched (Endpoint Security, logs, osquery). Most real compromises came through the gap between "on" and "watched".

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
md: Reversing is a loop of hypotheses: name what you think a function does, check it against the assembly and against dynamic behaviour, and rename again. Stuxnet's analysts needed months and domain experts; your first samples will need hours. The method is the same.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
md: Write for the reader who must act. The executive summary is for the person deciding whether to isolate fifty machines; the indicators and rules are for the people who will do it. Separate observed facts from your assessments, and say how confident you are.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: FP8 training with Transformer Engine in Megatron Core
md: Mismatched recipes fail quietly. For a run that converges slower than its BF16 baseline, the low-precision guide's first check is that the recipe matches the hardware table, because a mismatched recipe silently falls back to slower paths.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
md: Scanning finds what the list misses, and also things that are no longer true: exited processes and stale copies of live ones. A psscan-only entry with an exit time is history; one without an exit time whose PID is not in the list is the interesting case.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
md: Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
md: Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: A common misconception: "if it didn't crash, it worked". An out-of-bounds write that lands in another variable usually does not crash at all. The program keeps running with corrupted data, which is often worse than crashing.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. About two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, so moving new code to memory-safe languages removes most of the worst bugs at the source.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
